v.rationale: All three pass their own suites (impl-2: 22, impl-3: 33, impl-1: 36). All three stop a blocked user everywhere: each re-reads blocked_at from the DB on every request, rotates remember_token, deletes tokens, reset rows and DB sessions, and adds 'blocked_at' => null to the auth, reset-link and reset credentials. The shared probe confirmed a blocked token gets 401 without an Accept header and a remember cookie stops working, then login works again after unblock. A reset link issued before the block is unusable, and reset URLs use APP_URL even with a spoofed Host. The probes showed two real differences. First, the spec says non-admins get 403, but impl-3 and impl-1 return 404 for a missing {user} because binding or the ->can() check runs first. Only impl-2 handles this, by moving its middleware ahead of SubstituteBindings. Second, impl-2 and impl-1 validate 'remember' as boolean, so the browser checkbox default 'on' fails login. impl-2 ranks first: one minor bug, FormRequests and good middleware wiring, though its lockForUpdate transactions are unnecessary ceremony. impl-1 has the cleanest Laravel idioms (policy with ->can(), FormRequests, AuthenticationException, global web middleware with priority) and the best tests. It ranks second because it has both bugs and its forgot-password reveals which emails exist or are blocked. impl-3 has the fewest real bugs after impl-2 but the weakest idioms: inline validation, hand-built 401/redirect responses, missing return types and no throttling. All three blocked every attack, paged without repeats or gaps, and sent web guests to /login (JSON guests get 401). impl-1 and impl-3 use almost the same idiomatic design: Str::markdown with safe options in a model accessor, a newestFirst scope with an id tiebreaker, a Form Request, and associate() for the author. impl-1 ranks first by a small margin. It drops to third on idiom: inline validation, a static query helper on one controller called from another, user_id set by mass assignment, an unrequested JSON branch in store, a custom sanitiser class that repeats CommonMark's own protection, and a new converter built for every comment.

v.rationale: Both implementations meet the core requirements and pass their own suites (impl-1: 48 tests, impl-2: 19 tests). Each uses literal LIKE escaping with ESCAPE '!', allow-listed sorting, $hidden on the internal columns, a team-scoped exists rule and denyAsNotFound for foreign notes. impl-1 ranks first for three reasons. Its code is more idiomatic: queries go through relationships (team->notes(), make() plus author()->associate()), every route has a ->can() policy, and its factories return nested factories instead of calling create(). Its tests are much broader: data providers for crafted ids, wildcards and per_page values, plus a query-count test and a bearer-token test. Its sort scope also re-checks the allow-list as a second guard. Its one real flaw is integer:strict, which rejects form-encoded project_id. impl-2's controller builds the note by hand and runs an extra Project::findOrFail after validation has already checked the project. v.rationale: Both test suites pass (impl-1: 20 tests, impl-2: 23). I ran five probes against a real database queue worker: 422, cancel after dispatch, 503 then 201, a 201 with no id, and a rolled-back outer transaction. Both handled cancellations, retries, the exactly-once email and after-commit dispatch correctly. The difference is how they classify permanent errors. impl-1 retries every non-422 error, including 401/404 and a 201 without an id, for up to 8 exceptions or an hour. That keeps calling the partner for errors that never recover, and re-POSTs after the shipment may already exist, with only the Idempotency-Key header to prevent a duplicate. impl-2 fails fast on those, records the reason, and also refuses to ship unpaid orders. impl-1 does better in two places: its 422 path also lands in failed_jobs, and its mail-retry test is stronger. It also has more ceremony: WithoutOverlapping, nested branches and a bool-returning helper. impl-2's handle() is flatter and its tests use the fake-queue assertion helpers more idiomatically. Its weaknesses are small: a redundant SerializesModels and a mocked mail-failure test. impl-2 ranks first, narrowly.

v.rationale: The two implementations are nearly identical in structure: same attributes, a named limiter, a conditional claim in markAsPaid, a notified_at claim for the mail, and failed() that never downgrades a sent shipment. Both test suites pass (23 tests for impl-2, 20 for impl-1). Probes covered an end-to-end run through markAsPaid on the sync queue, a serialized job with a soft-delete between dispatch and run, a 200 response with an id, a 201 without an id, a pending order dispatched directly, and a 401. Both handled the end-to-end and soft-delete cases correctly. impl-2 wins because it classifies errors better. Permanent errors (401 and other 4xx, a 201 without an id) fail fast and reach ops at once. impl-1 retries them about 8 times over about 20 minutes, hitting the partner without need. impl-2 also checks that the order is paid before shipping. impl-1 shipped a pending order when the job was dispatched directly. impl-1 has some advantages: it accepts any 2xx with an id, its mail-failure test is more realistic, and it adds a unique index. Against that, it adds WithoutOverlapping ceremony, writes the 422 reason twice, includes an unused Sleep::fake, and has a weaker 422 assertion. impl-2's only real flaw is treating a non-201 2xx as a failure, which is narrower than the spec allows.

v.rationale:
All three suites pass: impl-1 43 tests, impl-2 35, impl-3 34. I ran throwaway probes against each and deleted them afterwards.

The deciding issue is the task's "well-formed carrier id" rule. impl-1 uses integer:strict, so JSON true, "1" and " 1" all get 422. impl-2 and impl-3 accept all three with a 201, and the response echoes carrier_id as true or "1" instead of an int.

On the list endpoint all three behave the same. The status and user_id filters are exact. paid=0/false finds the false rows. label_secret and unknown filters or sorts return 400. Rows from other or missing warehouses never appear.

- **impl-1 (rank 1):** Validation lives in form requests. The query is scoped through the warehouse relation. Users without a warehouse get 403. It has the most complete tests, and I found no bugs.
- **impl-3 (rank 2):** Close behind on idioms: form requests, an enum cast, a #[Scope] attribute scope and full relations. It has the loose carrier_id bug, and its whereRaw('1 = 0') guard for warehouse-less users appears twice.
- **impl-2 (rank 3):** Same loose carrier_id bug. Validation is done inline in the controller, including a hand-rolled validator inside the filter callbacks, and its filter errors are keyed without the `filter.` prefix. It also has no model relationships, no foreign keys, a status constant in place of an enum, and broad mass assignment.

v.rationale: I probed all three with direct DB inserts. impl-1 is the only one that refuses every malformed carrier id: with integer:strict, JSON true, '1', ' 1' and '+1' all get 422. It also rejects hostile filter values in a Form Request, scopes everything through the warehouse relation, and has the most thorough tests. impl-3 is close in idiom: a Form Request for filters, a #[Scope] that handles a null warehouse, store through the relation, and an enum cast. v.rationale: Both pass their own suites and share the same structure: a Form Request with mimes:csv,txt|max:5120, an invokable controller, a streaming fgets loop, and batched upserts with dedupe. The difference is how they handle hostile input. In impl-1, a quantity cell with invalid UTF-8 is interpolated into the error message, so JSON encoding fails and the import returns 500. It also stores non-UTF-8 skus. impl-2 checks UTF-8 and never echoes raw values, so the same probes return 200 with precise errors. impl-2 also rejects duplicate headers and relies on Eloquent upsert's timestamps instead of adding them by hand. v.rationale: The two implementations are nearly identical in structure: a FormRequest with mimes:csv,txt and max:5120, an invokable controller, a streaming fgets/str_getcsv importer with try/finally, batched upserts, and the same model, migration and factory. Both suites pass (impl-2 26 tests, impl-1 24). The probes separated them on handling untrusted files. impl-1 echoes the raw quantity into the error message, so a row with invalid UTF-8 bytes gives a 500 for the whole import, and it lets invalid-UTF-8 skus through to the database. impl-2 rejects invalid skus per row, uses fixed error messages, returns 200 with row errors, and rejects duplicate headers. impl-1 also sets upsert timestamps by hand, which Eloquent already does. impl-2 ranks first.

bugs: `php artisan db:seed` fails on a fresh database. DatabaseSeeder uses WithoutModelEvents, so Permission::findOrCreate never fires the package's cache flush. The in-memory permission list goes stale and `$role->givePermissionTo()` throws PermissionDoesNotExist (`posts.create`). Reproduced with migrate + db:seed.
